The Plague of Justinian. From 541 to 750 CE, a major bubonic plague pandemic ravaged the Byzantine Empire and Mediterranean region, killing an estimated 25 to 50 million people. The plague struck during Emperor Justinian the First's reign as he attempted to reconquer the Western Roman Empire. The pandemic weakened the Byzantine state and fundamentally reshaped the political map of the Mediterranean.

The plague was caused by Yersinia pestis, the same bacterium responsible for the Black Death more than eight centuries later. It spread via trade routes from East Africa and Asia. The first documented outbreak occurred in Egypt in 541 CE. The plague then spread rapidly to the Byzantine capital Constantinople, where thousands died daily at peak mortality.

Contemporary historian Procopius recorded the horror of the crisis. During the worst months in Constantinople, mortality was so high that mass burial became impossible. Corpses were dumped into trenches. The pandemic devastated Justinian's military campaigns to reclaim the Western Empire, draining the treasury and depleting his armies at critical moments.

The plague caused severe labor shortages and economic contraction across the Byzantine state. Agricultural production declined and trade networks weakened. Gradually, the pandemic faded by the eighth century, though sporadic outbreaks continued afterward. The exact reasons for its decline remain debated by historians. Yet the plague's impact demonstrated how a single pathogen could reshape the trajectory of a great empire and alter the course of history.
